title: Adobe Certified Professional explained: what it is and what it is worth
excerpt: Who awards the credential, how Certiport delivers the exam, which applications are covered, what Specialty Credentials require and how to prepare properly.
body_html:
Adobe Certified Professional is Adobe's own certification for its creative applications. It is the credential people mean when they ask whether there is "an official Adobe qualification", and it is frequently misunderstood, both by learners who expect more from it than it offers and by employers who have never seen one. This is what it actually is, who runs it, what sitting the exam involves and how to prepare properly.

Who awards it, and who does not

The certification is awarded by Adobe. The exams are developed and delivered through Certiport, the certification business that also handles Microsoft Office Specialist and several other industry programmes. You take the exam at a Certiport authorised testing centre; remote proctored delivery is available in some regions, so ask the centre what it can offer before you book.

No training company awards the credential, and that includes us. A training provider prepares you, gives you practice in the shape of the exam and can point you at a test centre. The certificate that arrives afterwards comes from Adobe through Certiport, and only a passed exam produces it. Be careful with any course that implies otherwise, and be equally careful with any course that guarantees a pass. Nobody can promise that.

Which applications are covered

At the time of writing, professional certifications exist for these applications:

  • Adobe Photoshop
  • Adobe Illustrator
  • Adobe InDesign
  • Adobe Premiere Pro
  • Adobe After Effects
  • Adobe Animate
  • Adobe Dreamweaver
  • Adobe Acrobat Pro
  • Adobe Express
  • Adobe Firefly

Each is a separate exam with its own objectives. Passing the Photoshop exam tells an employer nothing about your Illustrator ability, which is worth remembering when you decide where to start. Adobe updates the programme, so check the current list and the current exam objectives on Adobe's certification pages before you pay for anything.

Specialty Credentials

Above the individual exams sit the Specialty Credentials: Visual Design, Video Design, Web Design and Marketing Design. These are not separate exams. A Specialty Credential is awarded when you complete two related professional certifications. Visual Design, for example, recognises the combination that a print and brand designer is expected to hold, while Video Design recognises the editing and motion pairing.

That structure is useful when planning. Rather than collecting certifications at random, pick the credential that matches the job you want and work towards the two exams that sit under it. Two related passes read far better on an application than two unrelated ones.

What the exam is actually like

The exams combine knowledge questions with task-based questions performed inside the application itself. You are asked to do things, not only to recognise the right answer: open a file, apply a correction, set an export option, place an asset on the correct layer. That format rewards people who have genuinely used the software and punishes people who have only watched videos of it.

The objectives are grouped into domains that cover more than button-pushing. Expect questions on working with a client brief, on copyright and permissions for assets, on project requirements and document setup, on the vocabulary of the discipline, and on exporting for the right destination. Learners who have taught themselves from tutorials often lose marks in exactly those areas, because tutorials skip the professional context and go straight to the technique.

Exam length, question count, the pass mark and retake rules are set by Adobe and Certiport and are revised from time to time. Do not take a number from a blog post, this one included. Read the current exam details on the Certiport page for your exam before you book, and confirm the retake policy with the test centre so you know where you stand if the first attempt does not go your way.

What it is worth

Here is the honest assessment. A certification is evidence for people who do not know you. It does not replace a portfolio, and in a studio interview the portfolio will always be looked at first. What the certification does is settle a question that a portfolio leaves open: whether you know the software properly, or whether you produced six good pieces slowly with a lot of help.

It is most useful in four situations. If you are a student or a career changer with a thin portfolio, it gives a hiring manager something concrete. If you are applying to an agency or an in-house team through HR rather than through a creative director, it survives the screening stage where portfolios are not always opened. If you are a freelancer bidding for corporate or public sector work, it is a line item that procurement understands. If you teach, it demonstrates currency in the tool you are teaching.

It is least useful if you already have five years of published work and a network. In that case the exam fee buys you very little.

A caution about salary. You will find articles claiming a certification adds a specific percentage to your pay. Treat those with suspicion, particularly in the Sri Lankan market where the sample sizes behind such claims are tiny or nonexistent. Research pay the way you would research anything else: look at current job advertisements in your city, ask people doing the job, and check what agencies are quoting for the roles they are hiring.

How to prepare

A sensible preparation plan runs over six to eight weeks and has four parts.

Start from the objectives, not from a course. Download the exam objectives for your application from Certiport and turn them into a checklist. Mark each line green, amber or red. You now know what to study, and you can stop studying the things you already know.

Work in the application every week. Because the exam is task-based, reading will not carry you. Build real files. Rebuild a piece of packaging you have in the kitchen, redo a poster you have seen in Colombo Fort, retouch your own photographs. Volume of hands-on time is the strongest predictor of comfort on the day.

Close the professional-context gaps deliberately. Set aside one session for the non-software domains: client briefs, permissions and licensing, colour modes and resolution for a given output, file formats and their uses. These are cheap marks that self-taught candidates routinely drop.

Sit timed practice. Practice test software is sold alongside the exams and is worth the money if it stops you meeting the interface for the first time under pressure. At minimum, set a timer and complete a full set of tasks without pausing, then review only the ones you got wrong.

Three things people get wrong

"The course gives me the certification." It does not. A course prepares you; the exam certifies you. Any certificate of completion from a training provider, ours included, is a record of attendance and work done, not an Adobe credential.

"I should certify in everything." Two related exams that map to a Specialty Credential and to a real job are worth more than five scattered passes.

"It expires immediately." Certifications are tied to the version and programme rules in force when you sit them. Check Adobe's current recertification guidance rather than assuming, and keep your skills current regardless, because a five-year-old certificate with no recent work behind it convinces nobody.

Our Adobe courses are mapped to the published exam objectives and finish with timed practice in the same shape as the real exam. We will tell you honestly which objectives you are solid on and which need another fortnight of work before you book a seat at a test centre.
